slides.title: Korea's education minister steps down
body: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin **offered to resign** on Sunday, taking responsibility for confusion caused by last-minute changes meant to stop AI cheating on the national exam. President Lee Jae Myung accepted an hour later, Cheong Wa Dae, the presidential office, said.

slides.title: The test that decides university places
body: The College Scholastic Ability Test, known as Suneung or CSAT, is South Korea's annual college entrance exam. This year **551,864 candidates** registered, sitting it at 1,312 centres nationwide.

slides.title: 111 caught with smart devices
body: Authorities stepped up security, including unscheduled emergency alerts sent to detect hidden smartphones. **111 test-takers** were caught possessing or using smart devices. Cases included smart glasses, and a miniature camera with wireless earphones.

slides.title: Fears were already high
body: Worry had grown after the top scorer in Korea's national tax accountant exam admitted to AI-assisted cheating just before the CSAT. The ministry's misconduct committee will decide penalties **before scores come out on Dec. 11**.

slides.title: Tougher penalties are on the table
body: The government and the ruling Democratic Party of Korea suggested a **10-year ban** for AI-assisted cheating, possibly retroactive. Authorities are mulling a review of past exams and intend to offer rewards of up to 100 million won ($75,000) for reports.

facts.text: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered his resignation on Sunday, saying he will take responsibility for the confusion sparked by last-minute changes to prevent artificial intelligence-related cheating on the annual College Scholastic Ability Test, or Suneung.
President Lee Jae Myung accepted Choi's resignation an hour after he presented it, according to Cheong Wa Dae.

The government implemented several anti-cheating measures to prevent AI-powered cheating on the state-issued college entrance exam, including unscheduled emergency alerts sent to detect hidden smartphones.

The education authorities stepped up security measures against smart devices, leading to 111 test-takers being caught possessing or using smart devices during the exam. This included the use of smart glasses in one case and a miniature camera and wireless earphones in another.

This year's exam was marred by fears related to cheating with AI-powered technology, after the top scorer in the national tax accountant certification examination admitted to AI-assisted cheating just before the college entrance exam.
The Education Ministry's examination misconduct committee has been reviewing the cheating cases, and will decide on penalties before the scores are released on Dec. 11.
The government and the ruling Democratic Party of Korea have suggested extending the ban for AI-assisted cheating to 10 years, potentially applying it retroactively to this year's exam.

The authorities are also mulling a review of past college entrance exams for possible AI-assisted cheating, based on credible tips. Exam papers are mandated to be stored at test locations for at least a year.
A total of 551,864 candidates registered for this year's test, which was held at 1,312 examination centres nationwide.
It also intends to offer rewards of up to 100 million won ($75,000) for reports of cheating.
